title: Massage Franchises
one_liner: Membership-driven massage and spa chains are still expanding, but the post-pandemic growth story is now constrained by therapist supply, wage pressure and a more value-sensitive consumer.
overview: Massage Franchises covers franchised outlets that sell therapeutic, relaxation and specialty massage services, often alongside facials, stretching, skincare, retail products and gift cards. The category sits between discretionary personal care and complementary health services: consumers still cut back when budgets tighten, but 2025 survey data shows massage is increasingly framed as healthcare, pain management, stress relief and recovery rather than just pampering. The industry remains fragmented beyond the largest brands, but franchise systems benefit from brand trust, online booking, memberships, standardized training, local marketing and recurring revenue. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline forecast a young, fast-growing franchise niche reaching $5.2 billion in 2026; current public company and franchise-disclosure signals support continued growth, though at a more mature pace than the early rollout years.

key_stats.market_size: $4.5 billion estimated U.S. massage-franchise revenue in 2025; $5.2 billion 2026 forecast from the 2021 IBISWorld baseline trajectory.
key_stats.growth: 15.8% forecast CAGR for U.S. massage-franchise revenue from 2021 to 2026 in the baseline; broader U.S. massage therapy services were forecast at 5.5% CAGR from 2025 to 2034 by Emergen Research and 7.1% CAGR from 2024 to 2030 by Grand View Research.
key_stats.broader_market: $19.1 billion U.S. massage therapy services market in 2024, forecast to $32.5 billion by 2034 by Emergen Research.
key_stats.employment: 168,000 U.S. massage therapist jobs in 2024, with BLS projecting 193,900 jobs by 2034 and 15% employment growth from 2024 to 2034.
key_stats.consumer_use: In AMTA's July 2025 consumer survey, consumers received an average of 2.7 massages in the prior 12 months; 71% of massage consumers used massage for a health or medical reason in the 12 months ending June 2025.
key_stats.unit_economics: 2025 FDD-style disclosures cited median gross revenue of $897,288 for Elements Massage studios, $1,236,266 for Hand & Stone franchised spas, and $882,524 for MassageLuXe spas.

baseline_2022.market_size: $2.9 billion estimated U.S. massage-franchise revenue in 2022, derived from the 2021 IBISWorld revenue base of $2.505 billion and its 15.8% 2021-2026 forecast CAGR.
baseline_2022.growth: 15.8% estimated 2022 revenue growth under the baseline forecast path.
baseline_2022.establishments: About 4,335 establishments estimated in 2022, derived from 3,662 establishments in 2021 and the baseline 18.5% 2021-2026 establishment-growth outlook.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 9.5% EBIT margin in 2021 baseline, with profit expected to remain high through 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Franchisees earn most revenue from booked massage sessions sold to members and nonmembers. The strongest chains use monthly memberships, prepaid packages and gift cards to smooth demand and lift repeat visits. Additional revenue comes from facials, assisted stretching, skincare upgrades, aromatherapy, hot stone and deep tissue add-ons, retail products, cancellation fees and local promotions. Franchisors collect initial franchise fees, royalties, brand fund contributions, technology fees and sometimes supplier or product-related revenue.
cost_structure: The business is labor-heavy. Massage therapists, estheticians, front-desk staff and managers are the largest operating cost, with the 2024 BLS median massage therapist wage at $57,950 per year and personal-care-services median pay at $55,630. Other major costs include rent for retail-service locations, laundry and linens, oils and consumables, scheduling and POS software, insurance, local marketing, utilities and equipment. Ongoing franchise royalties are commonly around 5%-6% of gross sales in 2025-2026 disclosures, with marketing and technology fees on top. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline put industry profit margin at 9.5%, but 2025-2026 margins depend heavily on utilization, therapist retention, membership churn, local rent and wage levels.
major_players: Hand & Stone Massage and Facial Spa
current_dynamics: Demand is broadening from occasional relaxation toward recurring wellness, recovery and pain-management visits. AMTA's 2025 consumer data showed 86% of consumers agreed massage should be considered healthcare, while 79% said the primary reason for their last massage was health, wellness or stress related. Franchise systems are leaning into memberships, add-on services and medicalized messaging to offset consumer price sensitivity. Labor remains the main constraint: BLS projects fast 2024-2034 job growth, but therapist work is physically demanding and part-time schedules are common, making retention and appointment capacity critical. Competition is also widening from independent therapists, spas, chiropractic offices, assisted-stretch chains, recovery studios, mobile apps and emerging robotic massage.
whats_growing: Membership-driven formats, therapeutic massage, pain management, sports recovery, stress-reduction visits, skincare and facial add-ons, suburban white-space development, online booking, gift-card sales, multi-unit franchise ownership and robotic or automated massage pilots are growing. Hand & Stone reported more than 600 locations entering 2026, a $1.4 million AUV claim and 13 Q4 2025 spa openings; MassageLuXe reached its 100th spa in 2025 and reported continued franchise signings.
whats_shrinking: Purely indulgence-positioned massage, low-utilization single-service studios, operators without enough licensed therapist capacity, and mature chains with limited high-quality territories are under pressure. Elements Massage's cited franchised studio count edged from 244 to 239 between 2023 and 2025, suggesting optimization rather than rapid unit expansion. Consumers facing inflation are also more likely to trade down, pause memberships or stretch visit intervals when massage is positioned as optional luxury spending.
recent_developments: 2025-08: MassageLuXe announced its 100th spa opening in Fresno, California, plus new 2025 openings in Texas and Utah and two Atlanta-area franchise agreements.
2025-12: Massage Envy announced Aescape robotic massage at select franchised locations, with broader 2026 rollout expected in participating markets.
2026-01: Hand & Stone said it opened 13 spas and signed 12 franchise agreements in Q4 2025, entering 2026 with more than 600 locations.
2026-05: IFA/FRANdata reported health and wellness franchises were expected to exceed 99,000 units in 2026 and reach $66.4 billion of output.
2026-07: Grand View Research updated its massage therapy services outlook, estimating the global market at $22.2 billion in 2026 and a 7.3% 2025-2030 CAGR.
outlook: The franchise niche should keep growing through 2026 as branded chains take share from independents and add higher-frequency wellness services, but growth is likely to normalize after the early post-pandemic rebound. The strongest operators will be those that keep therapist schedules full, protect membership retention, add higher-margin facials or recovery services and use technology to reduce idle capacity. The main downside risks are wage inflation, therapist shortages, retail rent pressure, member churn, regulatory variation across states and consumer pullback on discretionary services. A reasonable 2026 view is continued revenue expansion toward the $5.2 billion baseline forecast, with longer-term growth closer to the mid-single to high-single-digit pace of the broader U.S. massage therapy services market.
one_sentence: U.S. massage franchises provide recurring, appointment-based massage and adjacent wellness services through branded local outlets, with 2025-2026 growth supported by health-and-wellness demand, medicalized positioning and multi-unit franchise expansion.

title: Massage Services
one_liner: A fragmented, labor-heavy wellness and therapeutic-services industry where demand tracks disposable income, healthcare referrals, stress management, pain relief, and spa traffic.
overview: Massage Services covers therapeutic and nontherapeutic massage provided by solo practitioners, clinics, spas, franchises, wellness centers, hotels, gyms, and mobile or corporate providers. The industry remains highly fragmented because licensing and training requirements create credibility but capital requirements are low, allowing many independent operators to compete with national brands. Baseline IBIS data showed therapeutic massage at 53.0% of 2021 revenue, nontherapeutic massage at 36.0%, and other massage services and products at 11.0%. In 2025-2026, demand is being shaped by consumers using massage for stress, pain, recovery, relaxation, and broader wellness routines, while operators face wage pressure, rent, insurance, booking-platform costs, and uneven insurance reimbursement.

key_stats.growth: 2025 industry revenue growth: about -0.4%; 2020-2025 CAGR: about 6.3%.
key_stats.employment: May 2025 BLS occupational employment for massage therapists: 107,540 jobs, excluding self-employed workers.
key_stats.wages: May 2025 BLS median wage for massage therapists: $26.34 per hour and $54,780 annually.
key_stats.consumer_penetration: 2024 AMTA consumer research: 29% of US consumers received a massage in the prior 12 months.
key_stats.therapist_supply: 2024 AMTA estimate: 329,000 to 332,000 massage therapists in the United States.
key_stats.spa_tailwind: 2025 ISPA US spa industry revenue: $22.5 billion in 2024, up from $21.3 billion in 2023.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 revenue: about $16.5 billion, derived from the baseline IBIS 2021 revenue of $16.221 billion and its 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 1.98%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 growth: about +2.0%, based on the baseline IBIS 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 1.98%.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2021 baseline profit margin: 7.6%; older IBIS narrative forecast industry profit margin around 9.8% by 2024.

how_it_makes_money.therapeutic_massage: 2021 baseline: 53.0% of revenue from therapeutic massage for pain relief, recovery, mobility, and health-related use cases.
how_it_makes_money.nontherapeutic_massage: 2021 baseline: 36.0% of revenue from relaxation, stress-reduction, spa, and leisure massages.
how_it_makes_money.other_services_products: 2021 baseline: 11.0% of revenue from specialty treatments, chair massage, add-ons, packages, and related products.
how_it_makes_money.channels: 2025-2026 revenue comes from walk-in and appointment-based sessions, memberships, packages, gift cards, corporate wellness contracts, spa and hotel partnerships, mobile bookings, and limited healthcare or insurance reimbursement.

cost_structure.labor: 2021 baseline wages were $5.251 billion, about 32.4% of 2021 revenue; 2025 wage pressure remains the main cost issue because service delivery is hands-on and hard to automate.
cost_structure.rent_and_facilities: 2025-2026 operators with studios, spas, or clinics carry rent, utilities, laundry, equipment, cleaning, and maintenance costs; solo and mobile therapists substitute travel time and vehicle costs for storefront rent.
cost_structure.supplies: 2025-2026 variable costs include oils, lotions, linens, sanitation supplies, disposable items, and retail products.
cost_structure.insurance_and_compliance: 2025-2026 costs include liability insurance, licensing, continuing education, background checks where required, and local compliance.
cost_structure.marketing_and_booking: 2025-2026 customer acquisition relies on search, reviews, social media, booking systems, gift-card platforms, memberships, and franchise royalties for branded chains.
cost_structure.profitability: Profit is constrained by therapist utilization, wage rates, room occupancy, rent, customer churn, no-shows, and the limited ability to raise prices when consumers treat massage as discretionary.

major_players: Hand & Stone Massage and Facial Spa
current_dynamics: The industry has largely moved past the 2020 closure shock, but 2025 growth is softer than the post-pandemic rebound because consumers are more price sensitive and operators face higher labor and occupancy costs. Demand is still structurally supported by stress management, musculoskeletal pain, sports recovery, aging consumers, and wellness spending. Chains compete through memberships, gift cards, standardized menus, and multi-unit franchising, while independents compete on specialization, trust, referrals, convenience, and local reputation. Therapist availability is a binding constraint in many markets because the work is physically demanding, licensing varies by state, and many practitioners work part time or combine massage with other income sources.
whats_growing: 2025 therapeutic and pain-management massage tied to back, neck, sports, mobility, and recovery needs.
2025-2026 membership and package models at franchise studios that smooth repeat visits.
2025 mobile, in-home, hotel, event, and corporate wellness bookings where convenience supports premium pricing.
2025 add-on services such as lymphatic drainage, prenatal massage, assisted stretching, aromatherapy, hot stone, and CBD-style topical upgrades where permitted.
2025 partnerships with spas, resorts, fitness clubs, chiropractors, physical therapy offices, and wellness clinics.
whats_shrinking: 2025 purely discretionary relaxation visits among lower- and middle-income consumers when prices rise faster than budgets.
2025 underpriced independent practices that cannot cover rent, insurance, marketing, and wage-equivalent owner compensation.
2025 low-utilization storefronts in weak office, mall, or commuter locations.
2025 operators dependent on one-time deal platforms where discounting attracts low-retention customers.
2025 practices unable to recruit or retain licensed therapists for evening and weekend demand.
recent_developments: 2024: AMTA estimated 329,000 to 332,000 massage therapists in the United States and reported that 29% of consumers received a massage in the prior 12 months.
2024: US spa industry revenue reached $22.5 billion, according to ISPA’s 2025 spa industry data, supporting demand for massage in spa and resort channels.
2025: IBISWorld-referenced public summaries put US massage-services revenue near $18.9 billion, with 2025 growth around -0.4% after a 2020-2025 CAGR of about 6.3%.
2025: BLS reported May 2025 median pay for massage therapists of $26.34 per hour and $54,780 annually, highlighting wage pressure for operators and income potential for practitioners.
2025: Major franchise brands continued emphasizing multi-unit growth, memberships, and facial or wellness add-ons to increase visit frequency and ticket size.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive but not uniform. Demand should benefit from wellness normalization, healthcare-adjacent referrals, aging demographics, sports and recovery use cases, and the spa sector’s continued scale. Growth will be capped by discretionary-spending pressure, higher labor costs, fragmented pricing power, inconsistent insurance coverage, and therapist supply constraints. Operators with strong retention, clean scheduling, high therapist utilization, specialized therapeutic positioning, and recurring memberships should outperform generalist providers competing mainly on price.

title: Material Handling Equipment Distributors
one_liner: Material handling equipment distributors sell, rent, install and service forklifts, conveyors, hoists, cranes, warehouse trucks and related parts for factories, warehouses, construction sites and logistics operators.
overview: Material handling equipment distributors sit between OEMs and downstream users in manufacturing, warehousing, retail distribution, construction, government and repair markets. Core products include forklifts, industrial trucks, conveyors, hoists and cranes, but the baseline industry is not just a new-equipment sales channel: in 2022, used equipment, labor charges and OEM parts represented 41.0% of revenue, giving distributors recurring service and replacement-parts revenue when customers delay large capex. Current 2025-2026 conditions point to a gradual rebound rather than a boom. North American forklift orders were tracking about 202,000 units annualized in 2025, up nearly 2% from 2024, with electric trucks at 72% of year-to-date sales through November 2025. At the same time, MHEDA members reported long decision cycles, elevated new inventory, flat rental pricing and persistent price competition, even as quoting pipelines, automation demand and early-2026 industrial-truck momentum improved.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 estimated US industry revenue: $61.0 billion, inferred from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $56.214 billion and the baseline 2022-2027 forecast path, adjusted for 2025-2026 forklift-order and equipment-investment signals.
key_stats.growth: 2026 estimated revenue growth: 2.4%; 2022-2027 baseline forecast CAGR: 2.0%.
key_stats.product_mix: 2022 baseline revenue mix: used sales, labor charges and OEM parts 41.0%; forklifts 25.6%; conveying equipment, hoists and cranes 20.9%; industrial trucks and tractors 2.3%; other 10.2%.
key_stats.forklift_market: 2025 North American retail forklift orders: 185,000 through November 2025 and 202,000 annualized, nearly 2% above CY2024; electric trucks were 72% of November 2025 year-to-date sales.
key_stats.capex_indicator: 2026 Q2 US private fixed investment in industrial equipment: $375.345 billion annualized, up from $337.999 billion in 2025 Q2.

how_it_makes_money: Distributors earn revenue from selling new forklifts, conveyors, hoists, cranes, industrial trucks and tractors; selling used equipment; renting fleet; supplying OEM parts; and charging for installation, integration, preventive maintenance, field repair and technical support. Margins are strongest where distributors bundle parts, service contracts, rental fleet, automation integration and consultative project work rather than competing only on new-equipment price.

cost_structure.purchases: Largest cost item; distributors buy forklifts, conveyors, cranes, hoists, industrial trucks, replacement parts, batteries and controls from OEMs, so steel, freight, tariffs and OEM lead times flow quickly into gross margin.
cost_structure.wages: Major operating cost because sales engineers, service technicians, installers and parts specialists are needed for complex equipment, automation and maintenance work; 2022 baseline wages were $6.458 billion.
cost_structure.rent_and_facilities: Branch networks, service shops, parts warehouses, yards and showrooms require meaningful occupancy and fleet-storage costs.
cost_structure.depreciation: Moderate for dealers with rental fleets, service vehicles, lifts, diagnostic equipment and IT systems.
cost_structure.marketing_and_admin: Includes local sales coverage, OEM program compliance, financing support, insurance, billing, collections and ERP/CRM systems.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 baseline EBIT margin was 4.4%, with competition and inventory carrying costs limiting pricing power.

major_players: Crown Equipment dealer and branch network
United Rentals and H&E equipment rental network
Regional independent forklift, storage-and-handling and systems-integration distributors
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Demand indicators improved: equipment investment rose sharply into 2026, business-equipment industrial production was up 5.4% year over year in June 2026, and forklift orders returned to modest growth in 2025. But distributors still face cautious customers, longer approval cycles, elevated new-truck inventories, flat rental pricing, private-equity consolidation, lower-priced competitors, skilled-labor shortages and tariff/material/freight volatility. The practical result is moderate revenue growth with better prospects for dealers that can sell uptime, automation ROI, electrification support and lifecycle service rather than just equipment units.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 warehouse automation, robotics, AMRs, controls/software and systems integration.
2025-2026 electric forklifts, lithium-ion batteries, chargers and battery service; electric trucks were 72% of North American November 2025 YTD forklift sales.
2025-2026 aftermarket parts, preventive maintenance, field service and used-equipment support as customers extend equipment lives.
2026 industrial and business-equipment capex tied to manufacturing, logistics, reshoring, data centers, aerospace, healthcare and grocery logistics.
2025-2026 consultative storage optimization, very narrow aisle systems, racking, conveyors and full-solution project management.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 purely transactional new-equipment sales where customers defer capex or shop aggressively on price.
2025-2026 internal-combustion forklift share, which was 28% of North American November 2025 YTD sales versus 72% electric.
2025-2026 rental pricing power in some markets as utilization and competition pressure rates.
2025-2026 simple phased storage projects where permitting, municipal scrutiny and buyer diligence delay execution.
2025-2026 margins on commodity equipment lines exposed to tariffs, freight, steel and aggressive competitor pricing.
recent_developments: 2025-01-14: United Rentals announced a $4.8 billion agreement to acquire H&E Equipment Services, adding a fleet that includes material handling equipment and roughly 160 branches across more than 30 US states.
2025-01-16: MHEDA’s member survey reported 60.98% of respondents expected 2025 sales to increase versus 2024, while automation, robotics, lithium products and AMRs were cited as growth niches.
2025-06-04: MHEDA released its 2025 Distributor Statistical Comparison Report covering revenue growth, gross margin, expenses, inventory turnover and receivables benchmarking.
2026-01-19: ITA reported North American retail forklift orders reached 185,000 through November 2025, implying about 202,000 annualized orders and nearly 2% growth over CY2024.

2026-04-24: MHEDA’s 2026 Business Scan said 2025 industrial-truck activity was slow with long sales cycles, but late-2025 and early-2026 momentum improved while inventory, rental pricing and labor remained pressure points.
2026-07-17: Federal Reserve G.17 data showed June 2026 manufacturing output up 1.1% year over year and business equipment output up 5.4% year over year, supporting industrial demand.
outlook: Revenue should expand modestly through 2026-2027 as industrial equipment investment, warehouse automation, electrification and aftermarket service offset cautious capital spending. The best-positioned distributors will carry technical service capacity, rental and used-equipment options, automation integration skills and parts availability. Growth is likely to remain uneven because large warehouse and manufacturing projects still face customer ROI scrutiny, permitting delays, financing sensitivity and input-cost volatility. A reasonable current case is low-single-digit annual revenue growth, with margins improving only for distributors that manage inventory tightly and shift mix toward service, software-enabled systems, batteries and project accountability.
themes: Warehouse density and very narrow aisle storage
one_sentence: The industry is a fragmented, aftermarket-heavy wholesale channel whose 2025-2026 recovery is being pulled by warehouse automation, electrification and industrial capex, while long sales cycles, elevated inventories, tariffs, labor shortages and margin pressure keep growth moderate.

title: Maternity Wear Stores
one_liner: Specialty maternity apparel stores remain a small, declining brick-and-mortar retail niche as births are flat-to-lower and maternity demand shifts to online, mass, department-store and resale channels.
overview: This industry covers brick-and-mortar retailers that specialize in maternity apparel, excluding online-only sales and department stores with maternity sections. The 2021 baseline placed industry revenue at $887.0 million after a 2020 COVID-19 collapse and a 2021 rebound, with the channel forecast to drift down to $867.7 million in 2026 as Destination Maternity exited standalone stores and demand migrated to omnichannel apparel retailers. Current 2025-2026 data reinforce that split: the broader U.S. maternity apparel market is much larger and growing through online, mass retail, athleisure, nursing-friendly and wellness-adjacent products, while the dedicated specialty-store channel remains constrained by a narrow customer window, declining fertility rates and high price competition.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 estimated specialty maternity wear store revenue: $867.7 million, based on the baseline brick-and-mortar industry forecast.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 estimated CAGR: -0.4% for specialty maternity wear stores.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2026 estimated profit margin: 4.2% of revenue, flat with the 2021 baseline outlook.
key_stats.broader_market_context: 2025 U.S. maternity apparel market estimates range from $2.82 billion to $4.67 billion because broader market definitions include online, mass retail and non-specialty channels.
key_stats.birth_demand_indicator: 2024 U.S. births were 3,622,673, up 1.0% from 2023, but the 12-month general fertility rate declined from 54.6 in 2024 Q4 to 53.3 in 2025 Q4 in provisional CDC data.
key_stats.ecommerce_pressure: 2026 Q1 U.S. retail e-commerce sales were $326.7 billion, up 9.8% year over year and equal to 16.9% of total retail sales.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated revenue: $883.5 million, derived from the 2021 baseline revenue of $887.0 million and the 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of -0.4%.
baseline_2022.scope: Brick-and-mortar specialty maternity apparel stores only; excludes online maternity sales and department-store maternity sections.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue by selling maternity bottoms, dresses, tops, undergarments and other pregnancy/postpartum apparel at specialty retail markups. The 2021 product mix was led by maternity bottoms at 35.7% of revenue, tops at 24.2%, dresses at 21.0%, undergarments at 13.7% and other maternity wear at 5.4%. Higher-end boutiques also monetize styling, workwear, occasionwear and postpartum/nursing-friendly assortments, while many legacy brands now rely on wholesale and e-commerce outside the strict store-only industry definition.
cost_structure: Merchandise purchases and inventory markdowns are the largest cost burden, followed by store labor, rent, fulfillment/returns support for omnichannel operations, marketing and payment/technology costs. The baseline reported 2021 wages of $125.0 million and profit of $37.0 million, with profit margin expected to remain 4.2% in 2026. Smaller premium stores can support higher gross margins, but clearance activity, short product-use cycles and online price comparison keep operating margins thin.
major_players: Target / Isabel Maternity by Ingrid & Isabel
current_dynamics: The channel is caught between two opposing forces in 2025-2026: consumers still value in-person fit checks for jeans, bras, workwear and occasionwear, but discovery, assortment breadth and price comparison keep moving online. The loss of Destination Maternity's standalone chain removed a major store base, while newer premium operators use a smaller store footprint as brand theater and community space rather than a high-volume national store network. Mass retailers and apparel chains capture budget demand with maternity capsules, and broader maternity brands are expanding into skincare, wellness, activewear and postpartum products that sit partly outside traditional apparel-store revenue.
whats_growing: Premium maternity boutiques, nursing-friendly and postpartum apparel, maternity activewear, sustainable fabrics, extended sizing, online marketplaces, wholesale partnerships, resale/rental models and wellness-adjacent maternity products are growing. Broader U.S. maternity apparel demand is expected to grow in 2026-2035 forecasts even as specialty physical-store revenue remains pressured.
whats_shrinking: Standalone maternity-only store chains, mall-based specialty apparel traffic, basic maternity tops that compete with oversized/stretch women's apparel, full-price commodity maternity basics and lower-priced specialty stores with limited online reach are shrinking. Birth-driven unit demand remains structurally capped, with 2025 provisional fertility rates below 2024 levels.
recent_developments: Jan. 2023: HATCH founder Ariane Goldman gained North American operating control of Motherhood Maternity, A Pea in the Pod and Destination Maternity while Marquee retained the IP.
Oct. 2024: Go Global Retail completed its acquisition of HATCH Collection through the Janie and Jack platform; HATCH reported two New York stores and 200+ wholesale partners.
Apr. 2025: CDC reported 3,622,673 U.S. births in 2024, up 1.0% from 2023, with a 2024 general fertility rate of 54.6 per 1,000 women ages 15-44.
May 2025: HATCH Mama launched on Ulta.com with a planned 2025 rollout to 370 Ulta Beauty stores, expanding maternity into wellness retail.
May 2026: Census reported 2026 Q1 U.S. retail e-commerce sales of $326.7 billion, up 9.8% year over year and 16.9% of total retail sales.
Jul. 2026: FRED/Census showed clothing and clothing accessories store sales at $27.864 billion in June 2026, indicating a large apparel base but not a recovery specific to maternity specialty stores.
outlook: Through 2026, specialty maternity wear stores are likely to remain flat-to-down, with revenue near $868 million and low-single-digit margins. The better growth path is not opening broad national chains but using stores selectively for fitting, community, premium positioning and local brand trust while capturing most scale through online, wholesale and mass-retail partnerships. Longer term, the broader maternity apparel category should grow modestly with athleisure, sustainability, workwear and postpartum extensions, but the dedicated brick-and-mortar specialty-store segment will keep losing share unless operators create a high-service reason to visit.
one_sentence: Maternity Wear Stores sell pregnancy and postpartum apparel through physical specialty locations, but the channel is losing share to e-commerce, family apparel chains, department stores and broader maternity lifestyle brands.
